Allegheny County by the numbers

Where are deeds recorded in Allegheny County, Pennsylvania?

Deeds go to the Division of Real Estate, which sits in Room 101 of the County Office Building at 542 Forbes Avenue in Pittsburgh. The division does the recorder's work in this county, and it also collects the state and local transfer taxes.

The counter keeps weekday hours of 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. For questions, call 412-350-4636 and choose Option 2. The recording page says most documents can be eRecorded online, so a title company in another city can submit a deed without anyone walking into Room 101.

A homeowner who sells in Allegheny County will usually never visit the counter. The title agent prepares the deed, records it, and sends the tax and fee payments that the division requires.

What does the Allegheny County Division of Real Estate charge to record a deed?

The standard recording fee for a deed is $200.00, and a mortgage costs the same, under the schedule effective January 1, 2026. Large documents add charges only when they pass 30 parcels or 30 indexed names.

Allegheny County recording fees effective January 1, 2026
Document typeStandard fee
Deed and deed related documents$200.00
Mortgage and mortgage related documents$200.00
Power of attorney$50.00
Notary public bond and commission$80.00
Financial statement$175.00

Source: the Division of Real Estate recording fee sheet. Each parcel past 30 on a deed adds $10.00, and each indexed name past 30 adds $5.00. Deed related documents include leases, rights of way, declarations of trust, oil and gas documents and sewage permits, all at the same $200.00.

How much is the transfer tax on a sale in Allegheny County?

It runs from 2% to 5% of the price depending on where the house is, and 1% of that goes to the state. The remainder goes to the municipality and the school district that cover the property.

The division collects every layer of the tax at recording, with one check for transfer tax and a second check for the recording fee. The county's own worked examples show the spread on a $40,000 sale:

  • A house in Shaler Township pays 1% to the state, 0.5% to the township and 0.5% to Shaler Area School District, for $800.00 in total.
  • A house in the City of Pittsburgh pays 1% to the state, 3% to the city and 1% to Pittsburgh School District, for $2,000.00 in total.

Scale those percentages to a real price and the difference is large. On a $200,000 sale, 2% is $4,000 and 5% is $10,000. Ask the closing agent for the exact municipal and school rates before the settlement statement is final.

When no price appears on the deed, or when an exemption applies, a Statement of Value on Pennsylvania form REV-183 is required. Certain family transfers can skip the form if the deed carries a sentence explaining the relationship. The Pennsylvania Department of Revenue, at 717-783-8104, handles exemption questions.

What formatting rules apply to an Allegheny County deed?

A deed must be typed in black ink on white or manila sheets, 8 1/2 by 11 inches or 8 1/2 by 14 inches, in a font of at least 10 points. Continuous paper is rejected.

  • Leave a one inch margin at the top of the first page for the certification stamp.
  • Print a name and a full address with zip code in the Record and Mail to area, outside that top margin.
  • Handwriting is limited to signatures, acknowledgments and a few listed exceptions.
  • Keep out tape, glue, staples, correction fluid and highlighting.
  • Double-sided pages are fine, though each side that carries text counts as a separate page for the fee.

The same page sets a formatting rule for the Certificate of Residence, and the county publishes content requirements for each document type separately.

How can I pay recording fees in Allegheny County?

Paying in person takes cash, a business check, a money order or a cashier's check. Personal checks, debit cards and credit cards are refused.

Firms that record often can open a draw down account in the office during business hours, which saves the trip to the counter with a check each time. The recording page lists online payment as an option, and the county posts a separate sheet for copies and their associated fees.

Anyone who sees an unfamiliar deed or mortgage filed against their property can use the county's web form to report suspected deed or mortgage fraud.

Where does the common level ratio come into a deed?

The Pennsylvania Department of Revenue issues a new Common Level Ratio factor for each county every year, effective July 1, and the Division of Real Estate links to it from its transfer tax page. The factor sits in the same list of helpful items as the Statement of Value, so a filer working on a gift or low-price deed will see both together.

The county's appeal board, meanwhile, lists 49.3% as the common level ratio for the 2027 tax year, applied to current market value in assessment appeals that began in September 2026. A ratio near 49% signals that county assessments, frozen to a 2012 base year, run well below current market prices. Ask the closing agent which figure belongs on the Statement of Value before the deed is signed.

What is Allegheny County like for someone selling a house?

Allegheny County covers 745 square miles, and the Allegheny and Monongahela rivers meet at Downtown Pittsburgh to form the Ohio. The Youghiogheny River joins the Monongahela at McKeesport, about ten miles to the southeast. With 130 municipalities, the county has more local governments than any other in Pennsylvania, and neighboring municipalities can carry different transfer tax rates.

The Census Bureau counted 1,225,035 residents in its July 2025 estimate, second in the state behind Philadelphia, and it lists 614,484 housing units.

Allegheny County housing figures from Census QuickFacts

Owner-occupied rate, 2020-202465.2%
Median owner-occupied value, 2020-2024$227,600
Median gross rent, 2020-2024$1,153
Median household income, 2020-2024$78,548
Building permits, 20253,191

About 35% of housing units are renter occupied, which matters when a seller owns a duplex or a house with tenants in place.

What should an Allegheny County seller check before the deed is recorded?

  1. Confirm the municipality and school district, since those two set most of the transfer tax.
  2. Review the deed against the formatting rules above so the division does not reject it.
  3. Decide who pays transfer tax; the Department of Revenue says both grantor and grantee are jointly and severally liable for the tax, so settle the split in writing.
  4. Choose eRecording or hand delivery, and for hand delivery plan on a business check, cashier's check, money order or cash.

Buyers of rental houses have a second step. Effective September 18, 2026, Act 29 of 2026 requires a new owner of non-owner-occupied real estate to send contact details to the county's chief assessor within 30 days of purchase, and a knowingly false filing can bring a fine of up to $500. A seller who is handing a tenant-occupied house to an investor can mention that duty to the buyer.

More questions about Allegheny County, PA Recorder of Deeds

What is the standard recording fee for a deed in Allegheny County?

It is $200.00 for a deed and for a mortgage under the fee sheet effective January 1, 2026. Parcels beyond 30 add $10.00 each and indexed names beyond 30 add $5.00 each.

Does Allegheny County take personal checks or cards at the recording counter?

No. The Division of Real Estate does not accept personal checks, debit cards or credit cards. It takes cash, business checks, money orders, cashier's checks and draw down accounts, and online payment exists for eRecorded filings.

Why is the transfer tax so different between Pittsburgh and the suburbs?

The 1% state share is constant, while the municipal and school district shares change by location. On the county's $40,000 example, Shaler Township totals 2% and the City of Pittsburgh totals 5%.

Can a deed be recorded without visiting Room 101?

Yes, the county says most documents can be eRecorded online. For hand delivery, the address is 542 Forbes Avenue, Room 101, and the counter keeps weekday hours.

Does a military discharge cost anything to record in Allegheny County?

No. Military service discharge papers, street or alley vacations and ordinances are listed with no recording fee.

Delaware County by the numbers

Where do you record a deed in Delaware County?

Deeds for Delaware County property are recorded at the Recorder of Deeds in the Government Center, Room 108, 201 W. Front Street, Media, PA 19063. The office keeps real property records back to 1789, the year the county was created from part of Chester County, and the phone number is 610-891-4152.

The counter is open 8:30am to 4:30pm, but documents are accepted for recording only from 8:30am to 3:30pm. A seller whose closing runs late in the day should ask the title company how it will get the deed in before the cutoff, because e-recording and hand delivery both follow the same recording window.

One office handles every deed, but each deed also touches a municipality. The recorder collects the local share of transfer tax for the township, borough or city where the house sits, so the municipality named on the deed shapes the final bill. Media sits near the middle of the county, which makes the Government Center a short drive from most parcels.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Delaware County?

A four-page Delaware County deed costs $117.25 to record under the fee schedule dated December 1, 2025. The $38.00 base fee covers up to four pages, four names and ten folio numbers, and the rest of the total is made up of county and state add-on charges.

Delaware County Recorder of Deeds fees, schedule dated December 1, 2025
Document (4 pages)Total fee
Deed$117.25
Mortgage$115.25
Satisfaction, release or assignment$84.25
Agreement, power of attorney or general miscellaneous$43.00
Certification (4 pages)$7.00

Breaking the deed total down shows where the money goes:

  • Base fee: $38.00
  • County Affordable Housing charge: $18.00
  • Judicial computer, access to justice and criminal justice add-on: $41.25, which rose by $1.00 on December 1, 2025
  • County Improvement Fund: $5.00
  • Demolition of Blighted Properties charge: $15.00

Extra pages on a deed are $4.00 each, and every name after the fourth or folio after the tenth adds $1.00. Veterans discharge papers are recorded free.

How much transfer tax does a Delaware County seller pay?

Most Delaware County sales carry 2% in realty transfer tax: 1% to the state and 1% to the local taxing bodies. A few places charge more, so the municipality printed on your deed decides the rate.

  • Radnor Township: local 1.5%
  • Upper Darby Township: local 1.5%
  • Chester City: local 1.5%
  • Upper Providence Township: local 2%
  • Everywhere else in the county: local 1%

On a $300,000 sale, the standard split is $3,000 to the state and $3,000 locally. The same sale in Upper Darby would be $3,000 state plus $4,500 local, and in Upper Providence $3,000 plus $6,000. Contracts often split the tax between buyer and seller, so read the agreement of sale before assuming who writes the check.

Chester City dropped its separate property registration form and $10 fee for sales after September 1, 2023. All Chester City properties now fall under the single 1.5% local rate.

When a deed covers land in more than one municipality, it has to say what share of the value belongs to each taxing body, using the Pennsylvania Statement of Value.

What paperwork and payments does the recorder require?

The office asks for three separate checks when a deed is recorded in person. Each has a different payee, so mixing them into one check will get the package returned.

  • One check for the recording fee, made out to Recorder of Deeds
  • One check for state transfer tax, made out to Recorder of Deeds, Agent
  • One check for local transfer tax, also made out to Recorder of Deeds, Agent

Every document needs a 1-inch top margin on each page, a rule announced on November 17, 2025, so the office can stamp recording data electronically without covering text. All documents are also subject to Solicitor approval before recording, which is worth building into the closing timeline.

E-recording submitters have a correction window. Fees have to be right, and the office told submitters on September 1, 2024 that they have until 11:30am the next business day after a month ends to flag incorrect fees. The county does not run title searches, so title work stays with the title company or an attorney.

What is the Common Level Ratio for Delaware County?

The recorder's 2026-27 Common Level Ratio factor is 1.83, announced on June 22, 2026. It applies to any document dated July 1, 2026 or later.

The ratio changes every fiscal year, so a deed dated before July 1, 2026 uses the earlier factor. If your document needs the factor at all, ask the office which one applies to the date on your deed.

How do you search Delaware County records and get copies?

Records from 1799 to the present can be viewed online through the county's public access site, and copies cost less there than in the office. Online copies are $0.50 per page, and copies bought at the counter are $1.00 per page. Electronic certified copies are $12.50 through the same public access site, while paper certifications are $7.00 for four pages plus $1.00 for each added page.

  • Property Alert: a free service that emails you when a document is recorded against your Property ID number
  • Return envelope: add $1.00 to a mailed request if you do not enclose one
  • Microfiche copies: $1.00 per page

Homeowners who worry about deed fraud can sign up for Property Alert before listing. It costs nothing and shows quickly if someone records a document against the parcel.

What should a Delaware County home seller know?

Delaware County covers 191 square miles and sits southwest of Philadelphia, where it is the only Pennsylvania county bordering both Delaware and New Jersey. Media is the county seat, Upper Darby is the largest township, and Chester is the main city on the Delaware River.

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts table lists 580,937 residents for July 2025 and 230,160 housing units. Median home value for 2020 to 2024 is $332,200, owner-occupancy is 69.6%, and median gross rent is $1,372. Median household income is $89,546. These figures run well above Elk County, where the median home value is $133,600.

The county had 216,946 households in 2020 to 2024, at 2.56 people per household, and the Census Bureau counted 217 building permits for 2025. About 41.9% of adults over 25 hold a bachelor's degree, and the mean commute is 28.1 minutes. Industry clusters along the river: the Trainer refinery and the Port of Chester sit on the Delaware shoreline, and the lowest point in Pennsylvania is at Marcus Hook, where the river leaves the state.

That price level makes transfer tax a real number in a Delco sale. A seller in a 1.5% township pays noticeably more than a seller across the line in a 1% township, so check the municipality before pricing an offer.

A four-page deed costs $117.25 under the December 1, 2025 schedule. Extra pages are $4.00 each, and names after four or folio numbers after ten add $1.00 each.

What are the transfer tax rates in Delaware County?

The standard rate is 1% state plus 1% local. Radnor, Upper Darby and Chester City charge 1.5% locally, and Upper Providence charges 2% locally.

What hours does the Delaware County Recorder of Deeds accept recordings?

Recording hours are 8:30am to 3:30pm, although the office stays open to 4:30pm. The office is in Room 108 of the Government Center in Media.

Do I need separate checks to record a deed in Delaware County?

Yes. The office asks for one check for the recording fee, one for state transfer tax and one for local transfer tax. Tax checks go to Recorder of Deeds, Agent.

Can I look up Delaware County deeds online?

Yes. Records from 1799 to the present are available online, with copies at $0.50 per page. Copies bought in the office are $1.00 per page.

What does the Chester County Recorder of Deeds do when a house sells?

The office in West Chester files the deed that moves a Chester County house from seller to buyer, collects the realty transfer tax due on that deed, and keeps the permanent land record. Until a deed is recorded here, the public record still shows the old owner, which can stall a buyer's loan or a later resale.

The county describes the office as the custodian of all land records and indexes for transfers, going back to 1688. It also records mortgages, satisfactions, powers of attorney, subdivision plans and notary commissions. The tax money it collects is passed on to the Commonwealth, the county's 73 municipalities and its 14 school districts. Staff cannot draft a deed, search for liens or give legal advice, so the drafting usually falls to a title company or attorney.

  • The search library is open until 4:15 p.m.
  • Fees must be paid at the moment of recording, and the office will not record an unofficial copy of a document that is already on record.

Bring a self-addressed stamped envelope with any paper filing. The county adds postage and a $2.00 fee when one is missing.

Deed in blank or relocation deed$183.50
Satisfaction, assignment, release, easement$81.75
Power of attorney$20.50
Miscellaneous document$40.50

Extras stack on top. A UPI costs $20.00 per number, a document that misses the PRIA formatting standards carries a $25.00 non-compliance fee, and each exhibit adds $5.00. The base fee already contains a $41.25 judicial administration charge set by the Department of Revenue.

What is the transfer tax on a Chester County sale and who pays it?

The county fee page puts the rate at 1% of the consideration or computed value, whichever is higher, with higher rates in three places: Malvern and Tredyffrin at 1.5%, and Coatesville at 2.5%. Ask the recorder for the combined state and local figure that applies to your deed.

State law makes both the grantor and the grantee jointly liable for the tax, and the Department of Revenue notes that certain family transfers and property passed by will or intestacy are exempt. Who covers the bill in a sale is a matter for the sales agreement.

  • Transfer tax is paid by separate checks, one for the municipality and one for the state, made out to the Chester County Recorder of Deeds.
  • Only business checks, cashier's checks and money orders are taken for tax. Cash and credit cards are refused for tax.
  • Recording fees go on a third check or other accepted payment.

What payment and paperwork rules cause rejected deeds?

Most rejections come from payment mistakes and missing page-one details. The recorder takes cash in person for recording fees only, and personal, estate and trustee checks are refused at all times. Checks older than 180 days are not accepted, no more than ten documents may share one check, and a returned check triggers a $25 bank fee on top of the $10.00 rejection fee for returned documents.

  • Type a valid UPI on the first page. A computer-printed label on page one is acceptable.
  • State the grantee's exact mailing address and certify it with a signature, as 16 P.S. Section 9781 requires.
  • Attach a Statement of Value when the deed does not state the full value, unless a family exemption applies. The Common Level Ratio factor, updated each July 1, belongs on that form.
  • For land in more than one municipality, show the local tax split in dollars on the deed.
  • Match every name across the caption, signature and notary acknowledgment, including Sr., Jr. and III.

What should a Chester County seller check before the deed goes in?

Start with the title trail. A prior mortgage that was paid off should show a recorded satisfaction, and the satisfaction, assignment and release category carries its own $81.75 base fee if one is missing. If the house came through an estate, the Statement of Value and the family-transfer rules matter more than they do on an ordinary sale, so the title company should review them early.

Also confirm the grantee's mailing address with the buyer. Tax bills are sent to the address on the deed, and the county asks that it be exact, current, legible and scannable. A deed sent in with a tax check from a personal or estate account will be turned away, so closing funds for transfer tax should be arranged as a cashier's check or money order ahead of time.

  • Order a copy of the vesting deed from the recording office if the seller's own copy is lost. Certified copies run $0.50 per page plus $5.00 for certification when made by staff.
  • Ask the title company whether the property sits in Malvern, Tredyffrin or Coatesville, where the higher tax rates apply.
  • Confirm the deed shows the correct UPI and not the tax parcel number, since the two are formatted differently.

Can a Chester County deed be e-recorded?

Yes. Chester County takes electronic filings through Simplifile and CSC eRecording, which is how most title companies deliver a closing package. For a deed that owes tax, the consideration and the state and municipal tax amounts must appear on the first page.

Each package is limited to ten documents, and a single document cannot list more than ten UPI numbers. E-recording is not available for deeds of correction, re-recorded deeds or Statements of Value with exhibits attached. Those go in on paper. Resubmitting a document costs a $10 return fee each time, and a document recorded in error is not refunded.

What does the Chester County housing market look like for sellers?

Chester County sits in the Philadelphia metropolitan area, with West Chester as the seat and Coatesville as its only city. The Census Bureau estimated 557,116 residents in July 2025 across about 751 square miles of Piedmont hills and valleys, with 217,440 housing units.

For 2020 to 2024 the Census Bureau reports a median owner-occupied home value of $485,600, a median household income of $127,208 and median gross rent of $1,763. Owners occupy 75.1% of homes. Houses in the south of the county, in the Brandywine and Octoraro watersheds, sell alongside suburban homes near the Main Line, so transfer tax can differ sharply from one township to the next.

More questions about Chester County, PA Recorder of Deeds

How long does it take to record a deed in Chester County?

Same-day recording is offered until 4:00 p.m. on business days, and e-recorded packages through Simplifile or CSC are the usual route for closings. Large plans must arrive by 3:00 p.m. for same-day handling.

Can I pay the Chester County transfer tax by credit card?

No. Transfer tax must be paid by business check, cashier's check or money order made out to the Chester County Recorder of Deeds. Credit cards may be used only for recording fees and copy requests, with a 3.5% in-person fee.

Do I need a Statement of Value to record a deed in Chester County?

Yes, when the deed does not state the full and complete value of the property, unless a family exemption applies. It is a Department of Revenue form and is recorded with the deed, so its pages count toward the recording fee.

Can the Recorder of Deeds correct a mistake in a recorded deed?

Not by editing it. A deed of correction costs $94.75 and needs a written explanation on page one, the book and page of the deed being fixed, a new acknowledgment and a Statement of Value. Deeds of correction cannot be e-recorded.

Is the transfer tax the same everywhere in Chester County?

No. The listed rate is 1% of consideration or computed value, but Malvern and Tredyffrin charge 1.5% and Coatesville charges 2.5%. Check the municipality where the house sits before you price a sale.

Berks County by the numbers

Where do you record a deed in Berks County?

Deeds for Berks County property are recorded at the Recorder of Deeds on the third floor of the Berks County Services Center, 633 Court Street, Reading, PA 19601. Counter hours are 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., Monday through Friday, and the phone is 610-478-3380. Documents can also arrive by e-recording, by mail or over the counter.

The office does more than file deeds. It also collects state and local real estate transfer taxes, affordable housing fees, judicial fees and redeterminations, records subdivision and land development plans, highway maps and real estate UCC liens, and swears in notaries. Every document recorded since the county was founded in 1752 is available as an image and index on its online search site, with original handwritten and typed books kept for 1752 to 1953.

Property owners can use the Property Alert tool, which the county offers as fraud protection for people who want to know when something is recorded against their address.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Berks County?

A deed, agreement, easement, lease or order of court carries a base fee of $88.00 for up to four pages, and every added page is $4.00. The county's fee schedule took effect on November 14, 2025, and a Statement of Value counts as an extra page when fees are figured. The base fee includes one tax parcel, and each additional parcel is $15.00.

Berks County recording fees, from the Recorder's fee schedule effective November 14, 2025
ItemFee
Deeds, easements, leases, mortgages and related releases or satisfactions (4 pages)$88.00
Powers of attorney, modifications, terminations and similar instruments (4 pages)$87.00
Each additional page$4.00
Each additional tax parcel$15.00
UCC financing statement$115.00
Clean and Green agreement$41.00
Subdivision or land development plan set$100.00
Certification$2.00
Copy, 8.5 by 11$0.50 per page

There is an extra charge to index more than 15 names on one document. Statements of Value that arrive through e-recording are charged a $0.50 per page copy fee for printing and mailing to the Department of Revenue.

What is the transfer tax rate in Berks County?

It depends on where the house sits. The Recorder's fee schedule lists a transfer tax rate of 5% in the City of Reading and 2% in all other Berks municipalities. On a $240,000 sale outside Reading that would be $4,800, and inside Reading it would be $12,000, before any recording fee.

How the payment is made matters here. The office no longer accepts cash or personal checks for transfer tax, an announcement dated December 6, 2022, and the fee schedule repeats that personal checks are not accepted. Overpayments of $10 or less are forfeited, and checks 180 days old or older are refused. Checks are made payable to Berks County Recorder of Deeds.

  • Ask your closing agent whether the title company will pay by company check or wire.
  • Confirm which municipality and school district appear on the deed, especially for Wyomissing Borough, where deeds must name Wyomissing or Wilson School District.
  • Read the purchase agreement to see who pays the tax, since the split is a negotiated term.

What does the Statement of Value need in Berks County?

A Statement of Value is required on every deed that does not state the full and complete value of the property, unless a family exemption applies, in which case the exemption has to be stated in the deed. It must also accompany easements and rights of way. The form is completed in duplicate under Department of Revenue rules, and it is the Pennsylvania REV-183.

The form uses the Common Level Ratio, which changes each July 1. For documents accepted from July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027 the Berks County factor is 3.12. Since the office treats the form as an additional page, include it when you estimate fees so the check comes out exact.

What documents does the Berks County Recorder reject?

Berks County is specific about format. Documents should be on white 8.5 by 11 inch paper at 20 pound weight, in a font no smaller than 10 point, with a one inch margin at the top and one inch margins on the sides and bottom. Legal size paper is no longer accepted, and light copies will not be scanned legibly, so use dark print and black ink.

  • A Property Identification Number (UPI) is required on every document that references real estate, and the grantee's mailing address must be exact, current and legible.
  • The written amount on a deed must match the numerical amount.
  • The acknowledgment needs the state and county, date, signers, notary signature and a clear stamp with an expiration date.
  • Do not include Social Security numbers or bank or loan numbers, since the Recorder may redact or reject the document.
  • The submitter's name and company must be typed in the Return To area, with a stamped, self-addressed envelope.

Documents received by 3:30 p.m. are generally recorded that same day and held until the next day before being returned.

What is Berks County like for a home seller?

Berks County sits in south central Pennsylvania, about 50 miles northwest of Philadelphia, and it covers 866 square miles with the Schuylkill River running through it. Reading is the county seat and the fourth most populous city in the state. The county was formed on March 11, 1752 from parts of Chester, Lancaster and Philadelphia counties and takes its name from Berkshire in England.

It is the largest of these four counties by far. Census QuickFacts estimates 440,072 residents in 2025, up 2.6% from the 2020 base, with 172,559 housing units and 163,236 households. The owner-occupied rate is 71.3%, and the median value of an owner-occupied home for 2020 to 2024 was $257,300, with median gross rent at $1,181. The county issued 582 building permits in 2025, which is more than the other three counties combined in this group.

QuickFacts shows 9.7% of residents as foreign-born and 21.3% speaking a language other than English at home. A document written in a foreign language has to be recorded with an English translation sworn or affirmed by the translator.

How do you get a recorded document back or obtain a copy?

The submitter decides where the recorded document goes, because the office requires a postage-paid, addressed envelope with each one. Title companies and attorneys often address it to themselves and forward it, and others address it to the new owner. If a copy never shows, check with the closing agent first, then request a copy from the Recorder.

Certified copies ordered online are $10.00 per document, regular copies from the website are 50 cents a page, and copies made in the office, other than your own home's deed, are also 50 cents a page. Credit card payments add a processor fee that is not a county charge. After a mortgage payoff, the lender has 60 days to file the satisfaction, and Pennsylvania lenders do not hold deeds, so no new deed will arrive.

What is the Berks County transfer tax on a home sale?

It is 5% in the City of Reading and 2% in every other Berks municipality, according to the Recorder's fee schedule. The office no longer takes cash or personal checks for it.

How do I add or remove a name on my Berks County deed?

A new deed has to be prepared and recorded. The office suggests an attorney, who can often file it too, and the office phone is 610-478-3380.

What is the Berks County Common Level Ratio for 2026 to 2027?

The factor is 3.12 for documents accepted from July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027. It changes every July 1 and goes on the Statement of Value.

Does the Berks County Recorder record military discharge papers?

Yes, recording a DD-214 and the Veterans ID card are free. You need to bring in the original discharge papers if you have not recorded them before.

Erie County by the numbers

Where is the Erie County Recorder of Deeds?

The Recorder of Deeds is a division of the Erie County Clerk of Records, and it sits in Room 121 of Erie County Courthouse I, 140 W. Sixth Street, Erie, PA 16501. The phone number is 814-451-6246, the fax is 814-451-6213, and the office takes email at recorder@eriecountypa.gov.

Its main job is to review, record and index documents that relate to Erie County real estate and to give the public and real estate professionals access to those records. Between 100 and 400 documents come through each day, so a deed with a missing page or a wrong fee can sit in a pile of returns.

The office acts as collection agent for the county, the Pennsylvania Department of Revenue, the Department of State, and the municipalities and school districts inside the county line. It does not run on county tax dollars, and the county says it brings in more revenue than it spends. Staff cannot give legal advice on your deed, so route questions about wording to a lawyer or your title company.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Erie County?

The base fee for an Erie County deed is $87.00 under the schedule effective December 1, 2025. Mortgages and a few other conveyance-type papers carry the same base fee, while smaller instruments cost less.

Erie County Recorder of Deeds base fees, schedule effective December 1, 2025
InstrumentBase fee
Deed, mortgage, excerpt of adjudication, declaration of acquisition$87.00
Mortgage satisfaction, assignment or release$59.75
Easement, right of way, land contract$59.75
Lease over 30 years$59.75
Lease under 30 years, agreement exempt from transfer tax, all other instruments$18.50
UCC filing$100.00
Subdivision or land development map$30.00

Add-ons apply when a document is bigger than the base allows.

  • Indexed names over four: $0.50 each
  • Pages over four: $2.00 each
  • Additional parcels: $0.50 each
  • Statement of Value: $2.00
  • Copies picked up, emailed or faxed: $0.25 per page
  • Certification: $1.00 per document

Each amount carries an asterisk on the schedule, so confirm the final total with the office before a closing check is cut.

Does Erie County charge transfer tax on a home sale?

Yes. The office collects Pennsylvania and local realty transfer tax on all realty transfers and sends the money to the Commonwealth and to the municipality or school district. The county points to 72 P.S. Section 8101-C and following, and 61 Pa. Code Section 91.101 and following, as the governing rules.

Some transfers are exempt. The county gives transactions between husband and wife, between parent and child, and between siblings as examples. Do not assume a family sale qualifies. The claim is made on the Statement of Value form, and the recorder reviews what the paper shows.

  • The Statement of Value costs $2.00 to record.
  • The Common Level Ratio printed on the 2025 schedule was 1.88 for July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2026.
  • The local rate depends on the municipality, so ask the office for the rate in your township, borough or city.

The 1.88 figure covers a fiscal year that has ended. Ask the recorder which factor applies to a document dated after June 30, 2026.

How do you look up Erie County deeds and get copies?

The Recorder posts an online index and images through Infocon, at www.infoconcountyaccess.com. The office also lists an E-Recording information page for title companies and other filers.

Because a fire destroyed the Erie County Courthouse on March 23, 1823, records accumulated before that date were lost. Researchers tracing a very old chain of title should expect gaps and should ask the office what survives.

Mail documents to Recorder of Deeds, 140 West 6th Street, Room 121, Erie, PA 16501. Include the right fees and a Statement of Value if one is needed, and put a return address on the package so the recorded deed finds its way back to you.

What would a typical Erie County deed cost to record?

A six-page deed with six indexed names and a Statement of Value comes to $94.00 before transfer tax. That is the $87.00 base, $4.00 for two extra pages, $1.00 for two extra names and $2.00 for the Statement of Value. The asterisk on the schedule means the office should confirm the total, so treat this as a planning figure.

The recording fee is small next to the tax. Erie County's base is $87.00, while a four-page deed in Delaware County runs $117.25 and in Elk County $92.75, so Erie County sits in the middle of these three. The larger cost in any sale is the realty transfer tax, which scales with the price rather than the page count.

On a $177,000 sale, the median owner-occupied value in the county, the 1% state share alone is $1,770 before the local share is added. The seller and buyer split that bill according to the sales agreement.

What other fees does the Erie County office list?

The schedule includes several items that come up around a sale. A notary appointment or renewal is $30.50 plus a $3.50 prothonotary fee. A storm water management map, planned community map or condominium plan is $30.00, the same as a subdivision map.

The county collects low-income housing fees and record management fees along with Erie County recording fees and the Pennsylvania writ tax. All fees and taxes are set by Pennsylvania law or local ordinance, so the recorder cannot negotiate them.

What is Erie County like for a home seller?

Erie County is the northernmost county in Pennsylvania. It has 1,558 square miles of total area, but 49% of that is water, because Lake Erie borders it to the north. It is the only county in the state that borders New York, Ohio and Canada across the lake.

Erie County has two cities, Erie and Corry, plus Millcreek, Harborcreek, Summit and Fairview townships and boroughs such as Edinboro, North East, Girard, Waterford and Union City. The county was created in 1800 and organized in 1803.

Settlement came late. The federal government resolved the competing New York and Pennsylvania claims to the Erie Triangle in 1792, which let Pennsylvania buy the land, and the state created the county from part of Allegheny County on March 12, 1800. For its first years Erie County shared a temporary five-county administrative unit, based in Meadville, with Crawford, Mercer, Venango and Warren Counties. Its first local officials were elected in 1803.

  • North: Lake Erie
  • Northeast: Chautauqua County, New York
  • East: Warren County
  • South: Crawford County
  • West: Ashtabula County, Ohio

The Census Bureau counted 265,832 residents in its July 2025 estimate, a 1.9% drop from the April 2020 base, and 120,762 housing units. The median home value for 2020 to 2024 is $177,000. Downtown Erie averages 26.4 degrees in January and 70.8 in July, and Corry, inland, runs a little cooler, at 23.8 degrees in January and 68.2 in July.

Beaver County by the numbers

What does the Beaver County Recorder of Deeds do?

The office files the deeds, mortgages and related papers that make a property sale part of the public record in Beaver County. It sits in the Third Street section on the first floor of the Beaver County Courthouse at 810 Third Street in Beaver, and the phone is 724-770-4560. Counter hours run 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Monday through Friday.

Recording in Beaver County started in 1800, the year the county was created, and every record has since been digitized. Besides deeds and mortgages, the office takes sheriff deeds, tax claim deeds, satisfactions, assignments, releases, restrictive covenants, leases, installment land contracts, Clean and Green filings and notary bonds. It also collects the Pennsylvania realty transfer tax and passes the local share to the municipality and school district.

If you own a house here, the office offers a free Fraud Alert sign-up that sends a notice whenever a deed or mortgage is recorded under your name. Others in the county may share your name, so check any alert against your own property before reacting.

Where is Beaver County, and who sells a house there?

Beaver County sits in the Greater Pittsburgh region, was formed on March 12, 1800 from parts of Allegheny and Washington counties, and takes its name from the Beaver River. It covers 444 square miles, about 9 of them water. The Ohio River cuts through the county and separates the southern third from the northern two thirds, and Beaver is the county seat while Aliquippa is the largest city. Beaver Falls is the county's other city, and the rest of the map is boroughs and townships.

Census QuickFacts puts the 2025 population estimate at 166,032, a drop of 1.3% from the 2020 base. The county counts 79,845 housing units and 72,257 households, and 75.0% of homes are owner-occupied. For owner-occupied homes the median value in 2020 to 2024 was $190,900, and median gross rent was $890. Residents 65 and older make up 24.8% of the population, which is why many sales here follow an estate or a move to smaller housing.

Getting around is easy for a buyer who commutes. The Pennsylvania Turnpike, I-376 and US 30 all cross the county, along with a long list of state routes. Climate is the hot-summer humid continental type, with January averages near 29 degrees and July near 73 in the Beaver and Rochester area.

How much transfer tax is due on a Beaver County sale?

The total is 2% of the value being conveyed: 1% to the state and 1% to local governments, split evenly between the municipality and the school district. The county notes that this value is not always the sales price. The Recorder collects all of it at the time of recording and will not accept a deed until the tax is paid.

The state and local governments do not care who pays, so the purchase agreement decides. On most agreements the buyer and seller split it, but the new owner answers for any shortfall if the amount is later questioned. Recording fees and both taxes can go on one check made payable to the Recorder of Deeds, and the office takes only cash or check.

What is a statement of value, and what is the common level ratio?

A statement of value is a state form, filed in duplicate, that either sets the value of the property or states the reason a transfer is exempt. The office requires one whenever the tax is not paid or the deed does not show the true value, such as a deed reciting $1.00 of consideration. State investigators can review those filings later.

Completing the form needs the common level ratio for Beaver County. The State Tax Equalization Board set the factor at 1.34, and it applies to documents accepted from July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027. Under 61 Pa. Code 91.02, the date of acceptance is presumed to be the date of execution written in the deed.

  • Exempt transfers named by the county include those between spouses, parent and child, grandparent and grandchild, siblings, and a stepparent and stepchild.
  • Other exemptions exist for particular situations, and the county points owners to an attorney or the Pennsylvania Department of Revenue.
  • If the state later decides the value was higher, or an exemption does not hold, the Department of Revenue mails a determination. You pay the added state and local tax plus interest to the state, and the Recorder then disburses the local share.

How do you record a deed in Beaver County?

You can bring it to the courthouse or send it by mail. In person, the office says review, receipt and scanning usually take 10 to 15 minutes, and the recorded original is mailed back within about a week. If a mailed package has not arrived after two weeks, the county suggests contacting the Postal Service.

Mailed packages need a check payable to the Recorder of Deeds for the right amount and a self-addressed stamped envelope with enough postage. The office takes no responsibility for postage that falls short or for returns lost by the Postal Service, and the FAQ advises against mailing cash. Most sellers never handle this step, because the title company or closing attorney files the deed. Ask whoever is running your closing to confirm the filing date and send you the recorded copy.

  • Documents that touch more than one municipality need the local tax split clearly stated.
  • Subdivision plans must be 18 by 24 inches or 24 by 36 inches, original on linen or mylar, and cannot be older than 90 days from governing body approval.
  • A veteran's discharge can be recorded through the Veterans Office in the courthouse basement, and the Recorder issues certified copies at no charge.

How do you look up a deed or a mortgage in Beaver County?

Beaver County indexes by name, not by street address or tax parcel number. To find a deed or mortgage you need the name of the grantor, grantee, mortgagor or mortgagee and the approximate year. Parcel numbers come from the Assessment Office, so a seller who only has an address should start there.

Every document in the office is public except military discharge papers, which are impounded. Staff can answer general questions by phone but are not permitted to run searches or give legal advice, so a title searcher or attorney handles anything deeper. To trace ownership backward, read the recital that follows the legal description, usually beginning with the word Being, and follow it through each prior deed toward 1800.

The county records deeds for land only, not buildings. Older deeds sometimes mention when a structure was built, and the price of a conveyance can hint at it, but the Recorder does not keep construction records. Check with the municipality for those.

What should a Beaver County seller do about liens and mortgage satisfactions?

Confirm that the payoff of your existing mortgage ends with a recorded satisfaction piece. The lender starts that step, and it may send you the forms. If it fails to file, you can bring or mail the original satisfaction piece to the Recorder with the fee on the current schedule and a stamped return envelope.

Before you list, pull your own name from the index and read what is recorded against it. Open mortgages, old easements and agreements show up there, and clearing a missing satisfaction is quicker before an offer than during the closing window.

  • Gather the last recorded deed and its recital.
  • Ask the Assessment Office for the parcel number.
  • Ask your lender for the recorded satisfaction on any paid-off loan.
  • Agree in writing who pays the 2% transfer tax.

Who pays the realty transfer tax when a house sells in Beaver County?

Centre County by the numbers

What does the Centre County Recorder of Deeds handle?

The Bellefonte office records the deeds, mortgages and related papers for every parcel in Centre County, and it acts as the county's agent for realty transfer tax. Its stated mission is to record, protect, preserve and reproduce the legal documents that relate to real estate here.

Official county land records begin in 1800, the year Centre County was formed. The office also records notary commissions, oaths and veterans' discharge papers, and it collects fees for the Affordable Housing Fund and the Administrative Office of Pennsylvania Courts. Each year it sends transfer tax checks averaging more than $5.6 million to 37 political subdivisions and six school districts. More than 10,000 people visit in person each year.

Where is the office and what are its hours?

The Recorder of Deeds is in the Willowbank Office Building, 414 Holmes Street, Suite 1, Bellefonte, PA 16823. The phone number on the county page is 814-355-6801, and the office is open Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.

  • Documents are accepted as close to 5 p.m. as practical, and there are no Saturday or evening hours.
  • Papers can be mailed in, provided every recording requirement is met and the correct fee is enclosed.
  • A deed that still needs its UPI can be sent straight to the Assessment Office, which stamps it and forwards it to the recorder.
  • E-recording runs through Simplifile and CSC.

Return time is usually one to two days, though holidays, volume and staffing can stretch it. The county advises contacting whoever recorded the paper if nothing has arrived after three weeks.

How much does recording cost in Centre County?

A deed or mortgage costs $71.25 for four pages and four names, per the county fee bill, with $2 for each added page and $0.50 for each added name. Fees are set by the Commonwealth through the General Assembly and can change.

Centre County recorder fee bill (source: Centre County Recorder of Deeds)
ItemFee
Deed or mortgage$71.25
UPI stamp from the Assessment Office$10.00
Easement, lease, right of way$59.75
Assignment, release or satisfaction$61.75
Mortgage modification or subordination$20.50
Plat or subdivision map, first page$40.00
Photocopy, per page$0.50

Cash, check or card is accepted for recording fees. Card payments add $3.99 or 2.95% of the transaction, whichever is higher.

What is the transfer tax in Centre County, and does State College pay more?

Yes. The county's tax page sets 1% for the state and 1% local on the consideration or value, except in State College Borough at 3%, Ferguson Township at 2.75% and Taylor Township at 1.5%. The state share goes to the Department of Revenue, and the local share splits between the municipality and the school district.

The office will not accept a deed without the tax due. In most sales agreements the buyer and seller divide the tax equally, yet the new owner answers for any shortfall if the amount paid is questioned. Unlike some counties, Centre County does not require separate checks for the state and local shares, and all checks are payable to the Centre County Recorder of Deeds.

For a house near Penn State's University Park campus, the municipality can move the tax bill by thousands of dollars on the same price, so confirm the borough or township before you set a net figure.

Which transfers are exempt, and when is a Statement of Value required?

The county names conveyances between spouses, parent and child, grandparent and grandchild, and brothers and sisters as exempt, and a transfer between ex-spouses is exempt too. Most nonprofit corporations are not. For anything unusual the office suggests asking an attorney.

A Statement of Value is a state form that sets the value of a property or explains why tax is not owed. The office forwards each one to the Department of Revenue for review. It is required whenever the true value is not shown on the deed, such as a $1 consideration, or when tax is not paid at recording. The county's own checklist adds that an exemption claim not based on family relationship must state its reason, and a deed on land in more than one municipality must show the local tax split in dollars.

How do I get a copy of a Centre County deed or check who owns a parcel?

Every paper recorded in the office is public except military discharges, so anyone can look at a deed or mortgage. A copy sent by request costs $0.50 per page, plus $1.50 if you want it certified, and the request should include a self-addressed stamped envelope. Give the full owner name, the property location and an approximate purchase date. A certified copy of a deed stands in for a lost original.

The county also runs an online subscription portal, WEBIA, that covers the recorder, register of wills, tax claim and maps. Records recorded before 1989 sit in separate Deed, Mortgage and Miscellaneous books, and everything since 1989 is in Record Books, which matters when a title searcher asks for a book and page.

Staff will not run a search for you or prepare a deed. If a surviving spouse owned the home as tenants by the entireties, nothing usually needs to be recorded at death, because the survivor explains the death in the next deed or mortgage. Other ownership forms can need different handling, so check with an attorney.

What mistakes get a Centre County document rejected?

The county lists ten instructions for filers, and most failures trace back to names, notary blocks or the UPI.

  • Names in the caption, signature block and acknowledgment must match exactly. Variants like John J. Doe and J Joseph Doe cause rejections.
  • The acknowledgment must show county, state, date, the person or officer appearing, and the notary's signature, seal and expiration date. It should not predate the document date.
  • The written amount must match the numeric amount on deeds and mortgages.
  • Every deed needs a pre-authorized UPI from the Centre County Assessment Office before it is recorded. Call 814-355-6721 with questions.
  • List the property's municipality, and every one if there are several.
  • Leave a one-inch by three-inch space for the recorder's stamp at the top of page one.
  • Include a self-addressed, postage-paid envelope big enough for the return.

What should Centre County sellers know about the local market?

Centre County is home to the State College metropolitan area, with Bellefonte as the seat and State College as the largest borough. Census Bureau figures put the 2025 population at 157,393 across about 1,109 square miles, with a 2020 density of 142.7 people per square mile. The 2020 to 2024 median value of owner-occupied homes is $323,500, and only 61.8% of homes are owner-occupied.

Median household income runs $74,291 and median gross rent is $1,207. Public school districts include State College Area, Bellefonte Area, Bald Eagle Area, Penns Valley Area, Philipsburg-Osceola Area, Keystone Central and Tyrone Area, so a seller in one township may be dealing with a different school district tax than a neighbor a few miles away. The county's Common Level Ratio was listed at 6.10 as of July 1, 2026.

More questions about Centre County, PA Recorder of Deeds

Do Centre County buyers and sellers need separate transfer tax checks?

No. The county's FAQ says it is not necessary to present separate checks for state and local transfer tax. All checks are payable to the Centre County Recorder of Deeds, and the office accepts cash or check for fees.

How much is the transfer tax in State College?

State College Borough is listed at 3% of the consideration or value, compared with 1% state plus 1% local in most of the county. Ferguson Township is 2.75% and Taylor Township is 1.5%.

Can I record a deed without a UPI in Centre County?

No. Every deed needs a UPI issued by the Centre County Assessment Office, sold as a $10.00 stamp, before it can be recorded. A separate check payable to the County of Centre covers it.

Can the Recorder of Deeds change a deed that is already recorded?

No. Once recorded, a document cannot be altered. A new deed showing the change has to be recorded, and a wrong name or description is usually fixed with a deed of correction prepared by an attorney.

Do I have to record a deed at all in Centre County?

A signed and delivered deed is valid, but recording protects the buyer. If it is left off the record, the former owner could still borrow against the property, and tax bills may keep going to the old owner.

Where is the Blair County Recorder of Deeds?

The median value of an owner-occupied home for 2020 to 2024 was $161,100, the lowest of the four counties covered here, and median gross rent was $885. Only 86 building permits were issued in 2025. About 24.5% of residents are 65 or older.

Wikipedia classes the climate as warm-summer humid continental. Altoona's record high is 103 degrees, and winters are cold enough that a buyer inspecting an older house will want to see the roof and heating system.

Photography and any image capturing equipment are strictly prohibited inside the office, so bring paper notes rather than a phone camera when you look up a record. Plan the visit around the time cutoffs and the document rules above. Bring a check, since no credit cards are taken, and the self-addressed stamped envelope for any mailed or dropped-off filing. How do you get a copy of a Blair County deed?

Records start in 1846, when the county was formed from Huntingdon and Bedford counties. Search them online through Landex or visit the office in Hollidaysburg.

Who records deeds in Adams County, Pennsylvania?

The Adams County Recorder of Deeds records them, from an office in the Adams County Courthouse at 117 Baltimore Street, Room 102, in Gettysburg. Staff answer at 717-337-9826 on weekdays between 8:00 a.m. and 4:30 p.m., and the office shuts for every holiday on the county calendar.

The same office acts as the Department of Revenue's agent for realty transfer tax and hands the money on to the state, the municipality and the school district.

Anyone selling a house in Adams County meets this office at the very end of the sale: the deed is signed at closing, then recorded here, and the recording date is when the new owner shows up in the public record.

What does the Adams County recorder charge to record a deed?

A deed or a mortgage costs $71.25 to record under the fee bill that took effect December 1, 2025. That covers the first four pages and the first four names, and a few add-ons apply after that.

Check only, with no cash taken, at the moment the deed is recorded. The county's fee bill describes a 1% state tax plus a local tax of the same amount, and it calls for three separate checks: one to the state, one to the township or borough, and one for the recording fee.

The Pennsylvania Department of Revenue explains that buyer and seller are both liable for the tax. Its page also lists transfers that escape the tax, such as certain family transfers and property passing by will or intestacy.

  • A Statement of Value is required whenever the tax is not paid in full, including when a family exemption is claimed.
  • When land lies in two or more municipalities, the deed has to state how the value splits so the local share goes to the right place.
  • The county's fee bill lists grandparent to grandchild and sibling transfers among the exemptions it recognizes.

The Statement of Value is a Revenue form with no recording charge at this office, and the county directs people with questions on it to the Department of Revenue.

Documents must relate to real estate, carry original signatures, and be properly notarized. The date on the document cannot come after the date of the notary acknowledgment.

It does not use the Uniform Parcel Identifier system, so no UPI fee is collected and no parcel number or street address is required on a document being recorded. It also sets no margin rules, and it takes both letter and legal size paper.

  • Include a self-addressed stamped envelope; finished documents are mailed back about two weeks after the recording date.

The courthouse lobby has public terminals for searching records, and a copier that runs on a button picked up from the Register and Recorder or the Prothonotary. There is no terminal inside the recording office itself, and photographing screens, books or microfilm is prohibited.

The office also runs a free fraud alert service called PropertyCheck, which emails or texts an owner whenever a document is recorded against their property. A seller who plans to hold other property in the county may find that useful.

Ask the recorder whether a title company can send a closing package electronically, because the office pages open to the public describe paper, drop box and mail only.

Carbon County by the numbers

What does the Carbon County Recorder of Deeds do?

The Recorder of Deeds is an elected county office that preserves the land records for Carbon County, from deeds and mortgages to easements and rights of way. When a house sells in Jim Thorpe, Lehighton, Palmerton or any other Carbon County town, the deed has to be recorded here before the public record reflects the new owner.

Each document goes through three steps: indexing the information into the public retrieval system, scanning, and verifying the index entries. The county stores one copy on its public system, Landex, and two archive copies on secure servers at separate locations. The office is also the collection agent for realty transfer tax and the court-related fees that go to the state, plus the Affordable Housing Program fee that supports income-based housing in the county.

How much does the Carbon County recorder charge?

A deed or mortgage costs $102.75 under the fee sheet effective November 17, 2025. That covers four pages, four names and one parcel number.

Longer documents pay more. Deeds and mortgages cost $4.00 for each page past four, other documents cost $2.00 per page past four, every name beyond four adds $0.50, and each extra parcel number adds $15.00. Pay the exact amount by cash, personal check, business check or money order. A wrong amount is returned with a $5.00 rejection fee, though an overpayment of $10.00 or less is kept by the county.

What is the realty transfer tax in Carbon County?

The county page states that the office collects 2% of the total consideration or the fair market value, and that money is split among the state, local school districts and municipalities. A Pennsylvania Statement of Value, form REV-183, is required whenever you are not paying tax on full market value.

  • All trusts require a Statement of Value.
  • Easements need one unless the grantee is a public utility.
  • A transfer out of an estate needs one unless full tax is being paid.
  • The form goes in duplicate and its pages do not count toward the page total.
  • A family transfer, such as a parent to children, must be typed on the deed if no tax is being paid.

Use the Common Level Ratio factor for the year your document is dated. For factors older than five years, call the office at 570-325-2651.

Where do I file and what is the deadline each day?

Carbon County takes recordings by mail, in person and through e-recording partners CSC and Simplifile. The office phone number on the county page is 570-325-2651. The county sets the cut-off for recording at 3:30 p.m., so a closing that wraps up late in the day may not record until the next business day.

Documents must pertain to real estate, be in English or carry a translation, and bear original, properly notarized signatures. Mailed filings need a self-addressed stamped envelope, and an office mailbox holder is asked to collect recorded papers at least weekly. Remote online notarization is accepted when the certificate says the notarial act involved the use of communication technology.

Why can a Carbon County deed be rejected?

The county's recording requirements run to 21 items, and the same few errors come up repeatedly.

  • The document date must be the same as or earlier than the acknowledgment date.
  • Grantor names, signatures and acknowledgments must match exactly, and the names should match the prior deed's grantee.
  • Reference documents must show the book and page of the earlier recorded paper.
  • The municipality, whether a township or borough, should be stated above the legal description. For land in several localities, show the percentage split for local transfer tax through the Statement of Value.
  • Deeds, mortgages, easements, releases and assignments need a signed mailing address certification, because that address tells the Assessment Office where to send property tax bills.
  • Notary blocks need the right venue, a legible stamp and a current commission expiration date.

How can I look up or monitor Carbon County records online?

The county publishes its records through Landex. Landex Webstore gives the public remote access to documents from 1988 to the present, and a separate Landex Remote service serves title searchers. Anyone can also sign up for a Landex Record Alert using a name or a tax parcel number, which sends a notice when a new document is recorded against that name or parcel.

An alert is a cheap way for a seller to confirm that a satisfaction of mortgage has been recorded after payoff, or for an heir to watch for filings against an inherited house. The recorder's staff can also help trace a property back through earlier owners and purchase prices, and can help replace a document that was lost.

  • A re-recorded document needs a new acknowledgment and new signatures.
  • Several documents filed together should be labeled, such as POA, deed and mortgage, so they record in the right order.
  • Sales agreements must list the full address of both buyer and seller.

Why do releases and satisfactions matter when selling?

A seller with a mortgage needs the lender's satisfaction recorded so the title is clear for the next owner. The county explains the difference. A satisfaction is used when the whole loan is paid off, and the lender signs a satisfaction of mortgage that is recorded to clear the title. A release, also called a partial release, is used when part of the property or one name is taken off the mortgage and the loan stays active on the rest.

Satisfactions and releases can reference only one mortgage each, and blanket documents are not accepted. Another rule affects trust transfers. Since October 1, 2024, the office no longer accepts e-recorded deeds into a trust, so those deeds must be brought in or mailed. For tax parcel numbers on agreements, easements, leases and rights of way, the county advises calling its GIS department at 570-325-8519 first.

What is the Carbon County market like for sellers?

Carbon County was divided from Northampton County in 1843 and takes its name from coal. Jim Thorpe, founded in 1818 as Mauch Chunk, is the seat, and Palmerton is the largest borough. Armstrong County by the numbers

Which office records deeds in Armstrong County, PA?

In Armstrong County the Register and Recorder handles it, from Suite 102 of the courthouse at 500 E. Market Street in Kittanning. One office combines three jobs: the Recorder of Deeds, the Register of Wills and the Clerk of Orphans' Court. The main phone number is (724) 548-3280.

Counter service for transactions runs from 8:00 a.m. to 3:45 p.m., while records research continues until 4:15 p.m. The office takes cash or check only, with no debit or credit cards.

The recorder's side keeps real estate records safe from loss, theft and damage. It records land documents, veterans' discharges, notary bonds and commissions, and powers of attorney that deal with real estate.

How does a deed get recorded in Armstrong County?

It can be recorded electronically or on paper. The office lists four e-recording vendors: Simplifile, CSC Recording, ePN and Indecomm. A title company that already uses one of them can send the deed without a courier.

The staff checks every document against a fixed list before accepting it.

  • The document date has to fall on or before the acknowledgment date.
  • Deeds and mortgages need a legal description that names the municipality, county and state.
  • The tax map number is required. It is not the same as a parcel number, and the Mapping Department, at (724) 548-3234, can supply it.
  • The acknowledgment needs the notary's signature, a readable stamp and the expiration date.
  • A Certificate of Residence must be completed and signed.
  • Documents with shaded areas are not recorded.

The office says there are no refunds, so the fee has to be right the first time. Multiple documents in one transaction must show their intended recording order on each page, and any re-recording expense caused by wrong order falls on whoever submitted them.

What does transfer tax look like in Armstrong County?

The office describes it as a 1% tax for the state and another 1% for the local governments and school district, paid on separate checks, with a third check for the filing fee. All three are written to the Recorder of Deeds.

A Statement of Value, filed in duplicate, is needed in three situations: the full price is missing from the deed, the deed is a gift or has no consideration, or an exemption is claimed. It is also needed for rights of way and easements. A transfer that is wholly exempt on family grounds does not require one, provided the relationship is written on the deed. The office forwards one copy to the Department of Revenue.

A deed that names a price of $1.00 triggers the form, because the real value is not shown. When land spans more than one municipality, the deed must state each one's percentage so the local tax divides correctly.

The state can later revisit a sale. If an investigator decides the property was worth more than stated, or that an exemption was invalid, the Department of Revenue sends a determination directly to the parties, collects the extra tax and interest itself, and issues a receipt for the recorder to file.

What fees and facts should an Armstrong County seller know?

The recorder's fee schedule is posted as a PDF on the county's Register and Recorder page. Ask the office for the current sheet before closing.

Common Level Ratio, July 1, 2025 to June 30, 20263.27

The Common Level Ratio changes each July 1, so the 3.27 factor applied to the year that ended June 30, 2026. Ask the office which factor applies to the date on your deed.

Record searches are by first and last name or by book and page. The office cannot search by tax map number or street address, and its staff do not give searches or legal advice.

Does Armstrong County offer protection against deed fraud?

Yes. The recorder runs a free Record Alert System through Landex, the recording vendor. Anyone who signs up gets an email whenever a document is recorded under their name, and businesses can sign up as well.

The same Landex site holds the county's records for people who search often, with a paid remote subscription for frequent users and a pay-per-document web store for occasional ones. Landex sets those charges, not the county.

Property owners who inherit or sell land in the county can use the alert to catch an unexpected deed or mortgage.

What are the Depreciation Lands in Armstrong County deeds?

The recorder's page explains that the Depreciation Land Program was created for soldiers, sailors and prisoners of war who served in the American Revolution and had been paid in Continental money that lost its value. Pennsylvania set aside roughly 720,000 acres in 1783 for that purpose, per the Depreciation Lands Museum, which the office cites.

Two framed prints of the Depreciation Lands from the Pennsylvania State Archives hang in the recording office. Staff will show a visitor how to use the computer system to locate an old document, though employees do not run searches or give legal interpretation, so a seller who needs a title history should hire a title company or attorney.

What is Armstrong County like?

Armstrong County covers 653 square miles of land in the Greater Pittsburgh region, with the Allegheny River running through it, and it was organized on March 12, 1800, from parts of Allegheny, Westmoreland and Lycoming counties. Kittanning is the county seat. Ford City sits three miles downriver and began as a plate glass company town. Parker, in the northwest corner, is an incorporated city of fewer than 800 people. Worthington, west of Kittanning on U.S. Route 422, is the farming hub.

Coal, natural gas, plate glass, brick and ceramics built the local economy, and gradual population decline set in during the 1970s and 1980s. January averages about 27 degrees in Kittanning and July about 73,.

Only 29 building permits were issued in 2025, so most buyers choose among existing homes. At the $157,300 median value, a combined 2% transfer tax would come to about $3,146.

More questions about Armstrong County, PA Recorder of Deeds

Where is the Armstrong County Recorder of Deeds office?

It is inside the Register and Recorder's office, Suite 102 of the Armstrong County Courthouse at 500 E. Market Street, Kittanning, PA 16201. The telephone is (724) 548-3280.

Can I pay with a credit card at the Armstrong County recorder?

No. The office accepts cash or check only, and it posts that rule in capital letters. Plan checks ahead for the state tax, the local tax and the filing fee.

Is e-recording available for Armstrong County deeds?

Yes. The office lists Simplifile, CSC Recording, ePN and Indecomm as current vendors, so title companies using any of them can submit a deed electronically.

What is a tax map number and why does a deed need one?

It identifies the property in the county's mapping system and has to appear on deeds and mortgages. It is not the parcel number. The Mapping Department at (724) 548-3234 can provide it if you lack it.

Do I need a Statement of Value to record a deed?

You need one if the deed omits the full price, is a gift, or claims an exemption, and it must be filed in duplicate. A transfer wholly exempt because of family ties does not need one when the relationship appears on the deed.

Who records deeds in Elk County?

Elk County deeds are recorded by the Recorder of Deeds, which shares an office with the Register of Wills and the Clerk of Orphans' Court. The delivery address is 250 Main Street, Ridgway, PA 15853, and the mailing address is P.O. Box 314, Ridgway, PA 15853.

Ridgway is the county seat, while St. Marys is the largest city. A seller who lives in St. Marys or Johnsonburg and mails a deed to Ridgway should allow time for delivery, and a title company will usually handle that step through e-recording instead. The office lists Simplifile and CSC as its current e-recording partners.

The office describes its mission as recording, protecting and reproducing legal documents that relate to Elk County real estate. It also acts as collecting agent for the Commonwealth, the local school districts and the municipalities when realty transfer tax is due. Records since 1843 are open to public inspection, except military discharges.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Elk County?

A standard Elk County deed costs $92.75 to record under the schedule that took effect December 1, 2025. That price covers four names, four pages and one parcel, and the schedule lists the fees as exclusive of state and local realty transfer tax.

Elk County Recorder of Deeds fees, schedule effective December 1, 2025
DocumentFee
Deed or mortgage$92.75
Quit claim deed or easement$79.75
Satisfaction or release of mortgage$81.75
Assignment of mortgage$81.75
Sheriff's deed or correction deed$81.75
Tax claim deed$79.75
Power of attorney$18.50
UCC filing$100.00

Extra pages are $2.00 each, extra names are $0.50 each, and extra parcels on deed documents are $0.50 each. A subdivision or survey map 18 by 24 inches or smaller is $50.00, and a larger map is $62.50.

The office accepts credit and debit cards through AllPaid for transactions that do not involve realty transfer tax or inheritance tax. AllPaid adds a convenience fee of 2.5% of the transaction, with a $3.99 minimum.

What does the Elk County recorder require on a deed?

The office has a short list of rules that title agents and do-it-yourself sellers both run into. Check the document against it before you send it.

  • Leave a 1-inch top margin on every page, because the office stamps recording data automatically.
  • Put the tax parcel identifier (UPI) on any instrument that affects land.
  • State the true consideration on every deed.
  • Pay state realty transfer tax with its own check or electronic payment.
  • Attach an original signed Statement of Value (REV-183) plus a copy if you claim an exemption from tax, unless the deed itself states the reason.

If the property lies in more than one taxing jurisdiction, the person recording must state the percentage of the property in each. Fees and taxes are due when the document is recorded, so a closing agent should bring payment with the package.

How is realty transfer tax handled in Elk County?

The recorder collects state and local realty transfer tax at recording, and the state share has to be paid separately from the other fees. The office page asks check payers to put the state tax on its own check.

Elk County's municipalities and school districts set their own local share, and the rate depends on where the house is. Ask the Recorder of Deeds for the combined rate for your township, borough or the city of St. Marys before you set a net-proceeds figure. The county's municipal list includes Benezette, Fox, Highland, Horton, Jay, Jones, Millstone, Ridgway and Spring Creek townships, along with Johnsonburg and Ridgway boroughs and St. Marys.

Heirs who sell an inherited house deal with the same office, which also issues letters and keeps wills. That is useful when a deed cannot be signed until someone has authority to act for the estate.

How do you search Elk County deeds online?

Deeds from 1864 to the present can be searched online, while anything older has to be searched at the office. Guests can view records with some information redacted. An account with a credit card lets you save or print an unredacted copy, and the price is 50 cents per page, the same as in the office.

Older books lettered A through Z need four zeros ahead of the letter in the search tool, for example 0000B. The search page also has a live chat link to the software vendor if the search tool misbehaves.

  • Records open to inspection: since 1843, except military discharges
  • Online searchable: 1864 to present
  • Older than 1864: search in person at the office

What estate paperwork sits alongside a deed in Elk County?

The Register of Wills fee schedule effective December 1, 2025 shows the filing costs an estate faces before a house can be sold. Letters testamentary or of administration start at $76.25 for an estate not exceeding $1,000 and rise with the value of the estate. The fee includes the $41.25 judicial computer and access to justice surcharge.

  • Probate of a will only: $15.00 for the first page, $2.00 for each added page
  • Short certificates: $5.00 each
  • Certified copy of a will: $10.00 for the first 10 pages
  • Inheritance tax return filing: $15.00
  • Certification of inheritance tax paid, issuing: $15.00

Ask the Register of Wills which of these filings your estate needs. A buyer's title company will want letters in hand before it closes on a deed signed by an executor or administrator.

What is Elk County like for a home seller?

Elk County covers 832 square miles, most of it wooded rolling hills, and part of the Allegheny National Forest lies inside it. The county was created on April 18, 1843 from parts of Jefferson, Clearfield and McKean Counties and takes its name from the eastern elk that once lived here. Bendigo State Park and Elk State Park are both inside the county.

The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 29,926 people, down 3.4% from the 2020 base, and 26.5% of residents are 65 or older. There are 16,968 housing units, 79.5% of occupied homes are owner-occupied, and the median home value for 2020 to 2024 is $133,600. Median gross rent is $719.

Elk County's assessment office says the county has used a 50% ratio since the countywide reassessment of 2005, which took effect in 2006. Its FAQ lists total county, municipal and school mills at 16.15 for 2025 and 18.40 for 2026 in its example. Highways serving sellers and buyers include US 219 and PA 120, PA 255 and PA 948.

Ridgway averages 23.2 degrees in January and 67.4 in July, so winters are long. A mean commute of 18.3 minutes and a density of 37.5 people per square mile show how different this market is from southeast Pennsylvania.

Yes. The office lists Simplifile and CSC as its current e-recording partners. Title companies usually submit seller deeds this way.

Can I pay Elk County recording fees by credit card?

Yes, for transactions that do not involve realty transfer tax or inheritance tax. AllPaid charges a convenience fee of 2.5% of the transaction, with a $3.99 minimum.

How far back do Elk County online deed records go?

Online deed search covers 1864 to the present. Deeds recorded before 1864 must be searched in the office at this time.
